title: Skydance Names Jay Askinasi Head of Ad Sales, Taps David Decker to Lead Content Sales and Ray Hopkins as Distribution Chief
description: David Ellison’s Skydance, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, continues to  announce senior executives in the new compan
body:
David Ellison’s Skydance, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, continues to  announce senior executives in the new company: On Thursday, the company said Jay Askinasi will lead ad sales for Skydance, David Decker will head up content sales, and Ray Hopkins will oversee distribution. 

	Askanasi and Hopkins will also serve as part of the Skydance Executive Leadership Team. The announcement was made by JB Perrette, the former WBD executive who is co-chair and chief business officer of Skydance TV and Skydance DTC, to whom the executives will report.
	

	With Askanasi taking over as head of ad sales for the combined company, Ryan Gould and Robert “Bobby” Voltaggio — who have served as presidents of U.S. advertising sales at Warner Bros. Discovery — will be leaving the company.


	“By combining our strengths and uniting our teams, we will build on the incredible legacies of both companies to serve audiences and partners in new and more innovative ways and shape an even more ambitious future,” Perrette said in a statement. “Jay, David and Ray are hugely talented and respected leaders with deep experience, strong industry relationships and a shared commitment to our partners and our people. There is tremendous opportunity ahead of us, and I look forward to working closely with them as we build the next generation media and entertainment organization.”

	Here are bios for each of the newly appointed execs at Skydance:

	Jay Askinasi, Chief Revenue Officer – AdvertisingJay Askinasi will serve as Chief Revenue Officer Advertising. A digital-first revenue leader, Askinasi joined Paramount as Chief Revenue Officer after leading global media revenue and growth at Roku. Previously, he served as CEO of Publicis Media Exchange U.S., where he oversaw major media and advertising operations. Across his career, Askinasi has developed expertise spanning platforms, agencies, data and advertising technology, with a proven track record of modernizing underused assets into high-growth commercial businesses.
	

	David Decker, President, Content SalesDavid Decker will serve as President, Content Sales. A more than two-decade Warner Bros. Veteran, Decker has led the worldwide licensing and distribution of Warner Bros.’ film, television, animation and digital content portfolios across major global platforms. Most recently serving as President of Content Sales for Warner Bros. Discovery, Decker has built landmark deals throughout his career.

	Ray Hopkins, President, DistributionRay Hopkins will serve as President, Distribution. Having joined CBS Corporation in 2013, Hopkins is one of the media industry’s most accomplished distribution executives, bringing more than 35 years of experience managing Paramount’s relationships with video providers, digital and streaming platforms and CBS affiliate station groups. He previously served as Chief Operating Officer of YES Network and has been inducted into the Broadcasting + Cable Hall of Fame. Hopkins is widely recognized for building durable partnerships and expanding the reach and value of premium media brands.

schema.headline: Skydance Names Jay Askinasi Head of Ad Sales, Taps David Decker to Lead Content Sales and Ray Hopkins as Distribution Chief

title: ‘Elsinore’ Star Andrew Scott on Why Movies Should Still Tackle the AIDS Crisis: ‘The Shame Lies With the Governments Who Ignored’ It
description: Rolling off the celebrated European premiere of “Elsinore” on opening night of the London Film Festival, Andrew Scott emphasized why movies should s
body:
Rolling off the celebrated European premiere of “Elsinore” on opening night of the London Film Festival, Andrew Scott emphasized why movies should still tackle the AIDS crisis, even as a new wave of LGBTQ films and series are tapping into lighter themes.

	“I welcome things like ‘Heartstopper’ and ‘Heated Rivalry’ and ‘Red, White & Royal Blue’ and all those things that are joyful. I really, really, really do,” said Scott. “And I think the fact that there’s lots of different types of gay drama, so to speak, in film and television is extraordinary.”
	

	But Scott expressed concern over a perceived reluctance to revisit darker chapters of LGBTQ history. “It troubles me a little bit because I think it speaks about people who perhaps don’t want to go back to a time when you’re talking about the AIDS crisis or you’re talking about when it was incredibly difficult for gay people,” said Scott. “And I think that sometimes comes from a place of shame. I don’t want to see that anymore (…) because the shame does not lie with the gay people.,” Scott said.


	“The shame lies with the governments who ignored the AIDS crisis and the stigma that was around people and the innate prejudice that was in society. So that’s someone else’s shame,” he continued. 

	Directed by Simon Stone from a script by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” stars Scott as famed Scottish actor and “Chariots of Fire” star Ian Charleson. In 1989, while already succumbing to complications from AIDS, Charleson replaced Daniel Day-Lewis in “Hamlet” at London’s National Theatre after the actor had walked off stage mid-performance, never to return to the production. Charleson received rave reviews, but died just seven weeks after bowing out. 
	

	Last night, following the premiere, Scott came on stage and called up the real-life individuals portrayed in the film alongside the actors playing them, including the National Theatre’s stage doorkeeper for 46 years, Linda Tolhurst (played by Monica Dolan), its long-serving dresser Ralph Mills (Paul Chahidi), and director and Charleson’s close friend Sean Mathias (Matthew Beard). He also brought on stage the pioneering HIV/AIDS consultant Dr. Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman), who drew a standing ovation.

	“It’s difficult to underestimate the impact this person had on the development of treatment for people suffering with HIV and AIDS,” said Scott. “To our mind, she is a true life hero.”

	“Elsinore,” which is backed by Studiocanal, world premiered at Telluride to stellar reviews and expected to turn up in the Awards Season.

schema.headline: ‘Elsinore’ Star Andrew Scott on Why Movies Should Still Tackle the AIDS Crisis: ‘The Shame Lies With the Governments Who Ignored’ It

title: Will Geese Rock the Grammy Nominations? Here’s Why They Should …
description:

body:
It’s no secret that traditional rock music has been in a sorry state for most of the 21st century. 

	While subgenres like alternative and metal have thrived, straight-ahead rock has almost seemed like a museum piece, with much of its sound and energy migrating to Nashville and morphing with country. Sure, the Rolling Stones, Paul McCartney and U2 are still among the top touring acts in the world, but they and much of their audience are approaching retirement age, if not well past it.
	

	As this century progressed and the impact of the White Stripes and the Strokes — the last two rock bands who truly shaped culture — began to fade, the Grammy rock nominees reflected this conundrum, mixing aging classic rockers like Bruce Springsteen, U2, AC/DC, Tom Petty and even Led Zeppelin (who broke up in 1980 but won best rock album in 2014 for a reunion-concert recording of half-century-old songs) with newer classic rockers like Foo Fighters, Alabama Shakes and the Black Keys, throwing in relative newbies like Radiohead (who seem to be trying very hard not to be a rock band), Kings of Leon, Arctic Monkeys, Twenty One Pilots and Jack White. 


	Yet seemingly out of desperation, the nominees also have included total head-scratchers like Coldplay, Florence + the Machine, Matchbox Twenty, the Eagles — the fuckin’ Eagles, man! — and even Leonard Cohen, who inexplicably won Best Rock Performance in 2017 (albeit posthumously, sadly depriving the world of what certainly would have been a memorably bemused acceptance speech).

	Part of this was due to the innovation in popular music moving to the hip-hop, pop and dance worlds and the Grammys’ genrefication of rock into metal, Americana and alternative categories. But mostly it was because traditional rock music was basically stagnant. Considering the popularity of Schools of Rock and the millions of parents who bought their children guitars and drums and basically raised them on rock, it’s a strange conundrum.
	

	To its credit, in recent years the Grammys have worked strenuously to liven up the category, recognizing relatively new upstarts like emo innovators Turnstile and the bruising postpunk act Idles and Irish brawlers Fontaines D.C. (as nominees — the usual suspects usually win). While those bands have breathed some new life into the genre, they stopped well short of the cultural spark that the White Stripes or Strokes, let alone Nirvana and the Ramones, ignited.

	Yet the Grammys have the opportunity to recognize arguably the most exciting rock band to come along in many years: Brooklyn quartet Geese, who fuse 21st century innovation with rock tradition in ways that no other band really has — and crucially, their sound is genuinely rebellious in a way that one rarely hears in rock music these days. 

	In past decades, rock and roll was about rebellion, not just culturally but sonically: The first time people heard or saw Little Richard, Mick Jagger, Ozzy Osbourne, Iggy Pop, Johnny Rotten or Stephen Malkmus, it not only felt disruptive and a little frightening, but their unusual voices might have been offputting at first. None are conventionally “good singers,” and their sound took some getting used to, like coffee or whisky.

	Without equating him with those icons, Geese frontman Cameron Winter continues in that not-sure-you-like-it-at-first tradition, with a singing voice that careens between bellowing and nonsensical exhortations (“Get out! Get under!”) and snarky asides, almost never singing in a style one would consider conventional. The band’s music goes down more smoothly but is just as challenging: All four are fiery and skilled musicians, blazing through their songs’ unusual structures and angular riffs with ease. And their choice of covers shows how deeply they’ve studied the classics — Pink Floyd’s “Interstellar Overdrive,” the Stooges “TV Eye,” the Ramones’ “Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue” — as well as their wry humor: they’ve played both the New Radicals’ “You Get What You Give” and Justin Bieber’s “Baby” with (relatively) straight faces. 

	And perhaps most of all, they’re a real band — Geese formed a decade ago, when the members were in high school — that came up in a modern version of the traditional way, with School of Rock classes, sparsely attended early gigs and hard-to-find early recordings (and parental approval). And during the exploratory moments of their blazing live sets, the bandmembers respond to each others’ playing in ways that you hear from the most-seasoned groups. 
	

	Along with a potential best new artist Grammy nom, Geese could slot into rock or alternative categories, and the group’s label confirms that they have been submitted for all three. Best new artist may be a long shot in the year of Ella Langley, but that aside, there’s no question in our minds where they belong: The rock categories include best album (won last year by Ozzy Osbourne), best song (Brandi Carlile’s “Broken Horses”) and best performance (the Foo Fighters’ “Making a Fire”). The average age of last year’s rock winners was 59; the members of Geese are 23 or 24. 

	Grammy voters, respectfully, the next big rock band is here. Show the music world that you see it.

schema.headline: Will Geese Rock the Grammy Nominations? Here’s Why They Should …

title: Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on ‘The Social Reckoning’: Getting Inside a Whistleblower’s Mind, Jeremy Strong’s ‘Antihero’ Zuckerberg and Why Trump is the Movie’s Voldemort
description:

body:
SPOILER WARNING: This interview contains plot points, including some spoilers, for “The Social Reckoning,” opening in theaters on Oct. 9.

	“The Social Reckoning” is many things — but those expecting a direct follow-up to 2010’s “The Social Network” may be surprised.

	That earlier film, which earned Aaron Sorkin an Oscar for its screenplay, closely followed the emotional trajectory of Mark Zuckerberg (played then by Jesse Eisenberg) as he first created Facebook and then fought to defend himself against charges of IP theft. Now, “The Social Reckoning” confronts the world Facebook has made, with Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) a supporting character in the story of Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a mid-level Facebook employee who decides to become an unlikely whistleblower.
	

	Haugen’s charges, in our world, became “The Facebook Files,” published in 2021 by Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and sharing with the world the company’s seeming indifference to its spread of misinformation and its negative impacts on mental health among young users. (Jeremy Allen White plays Horwitz in the film.) Madison’s tracking of Haugen’s steps from believer in Facebook’s mission as a member of its do-gooding, soon-to-be-dissolved civic integrity team to burn-it-down apostate is compelling in part because of the difference between this character and the Zuck we once knew. In Sorkin’s writing, Zuckerberg sees himself as a figure with the power to shift the culture. Haugen wants no such thing — but may have ended up doing so anyway.


	The film represents a hinge point for both its writer-director and its star: Sorkin takes over directing duties from “The Social Network” helmer David Fincher, and the new film is the most anticipated of his four efforts so far behind the camera. For Madison, it’s her first film since her emergence as a star (and her Oscar win) with 2024’s “Anora” — a role whose emotional arc, from brashness to shy isolation, is more or less the opposite of Frances’.
	

	In their one interview together promoting “The Social Reckoning,” out Oct. 9, Sorkin and Madison spoke about the trickiness of trying to make a crowd-pleaser about contentious issues, Madison’s inhabiting Haugen without yet having met her, and what Madison learned sharing a scene with the famously committed Strong.
	
		I noted that multiple politicians are part of this story — I caught references to Donald Trump (obviously, given that the film depicts the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol), and to Bernie Sanders — but that they’re never mentioned by name. What did this lack of specific reference add to the way the story was told?	

	Sorkin: Is it OK if I … because I was the one who did that?

	Madison: Yes!

	Sorkin: Just because I was the one who did that. You didn’t get to decide.

	Madison: Take it. 

	Sorkin: Two things: I didn’t want the distraction. And I don’t like for a movie to feel timely. I want it to feel timeless, and so a few years from now, 10 years from now, 50 years from now, I don’t want it to feel like you can only appreciate this movie if you were involved with the news back in 2026.
	
		Mikey, Aaron writes famously rhythmic dialogue meant to be delivered with verve and speed — and delivered precisely as written. What was it like immersing yourself in that?	

	Madison: Reading his script, I was aware of it in some way, and also because of his work that I had seen and loved. But then being on set for my first day working with Jeremy Allen White, we had this monster of a scene with a ton of dialogue. It was quite dense, and a lot of information that we were going back and forth with. That was the first day where I was really like, OK, yes, this is like a different beast than anything that I’ve experienced before, but challenging, interesting, very different. I was very welcoming toward it because as an actor, it’s interesting to be experiencing all different kinds of work.
	
		You’re playing a real person, Frances Haugen, and you hadn’t met her when you shot the role. Have you met her by now?	

	Madison: I’m meeting her very soon, and I’m really looking forward to it. I think we’ll have a lot to talk about, and also I just want to share my admiration for her in person. We’ve been sending some notes to each other back and forth via email, but this will be the first time like face-to-face.
	

	Sorkin: You’re meeting her tonight. [Haugen and Madison walked the red carpet together at the New York premiere of “The Social Reckoning” on Oct. 4, the same day this interview took place.]

	Madison: Yes, I am. But then we’re also meeting another time. Yeah, I’m playing a character based off of a real person, and we’re following her story and the facts of what happened very closely and specifically and honestly.

	But in terms of building a character, it was one that I built purely from the ground up. Of course I wanted to meet her — I found her to be amazing. But I was also concerned that it would interfere with Aaron’s and my vision, and I didn’t want it to alter the character that I had created. And so I decided to just hold off a little bit until I reached out to her.
	
		This film has a similar device at its opening to “The Social Network”: A vignette plays out that informs everything that comes after. Then, it was Rooney Mara’s character dumping Mark Zuckerberg. Now, it’s a young woman [Portia Doubleday] whose routine traffic stop by the cops turns into a parable about how social media has poisoned our brains. It ends up being hugely important to the movie. What inspired this story-in-miniature?	

	Sorkin: I had been spending a lot of time with Frances — many hours over a period of many months, and the same thing with Jeff Horwitz. What I had was a lot of information, but I couldn’t find the shape of a movie yet, until I asked Frances what was the inciting action. One day you weren’t a Facebook whistleblower. The next day you were. What changed? And she said, “I had a friend who had been radicalized by spending too much time on Facebook.” And I began to imagine the opening scene.
	
		I didn’t realize that was drawn from life.	

	Sorkin: As is the opening scene in “The Social Network,” by the way.
	
		Frances Haugen opened up to journalists and testified before Congress, but opening up to a dramatist strikes me as a different thing altogether. What was that process like for you?	

	Sorkin: I really have to hand it to Frances. I don’t know how many of us would have been happy about having a movie made about us — putting our life in the hands of a complete stranger, whose wishes and agenda may not be the same as ours. I would talk to her about that from time to time. Are you OK with this? Are you OK with that? And what was important to her was getting the word out about what she had discovered.
	
	
		I think of “The Social Network” as a character study of Mark Zuckerberg. Here, though, he’s such a malign presence and, for me, a lot of his complication seems to have been sanded away by his success. Aaron, how did you talk to Jeremy Strong about playing him now? No actor wants to see the person they’re playing as irredeemable.	

	Sorkin: Yeah, sure, and neither of us did. The character of Mark Zuckerberg has a different function in this film than he did in “The Social Network.” He was an antihero, but he was the protagonist in “The Social Network,” and Frances is the protagonist in “The Social Reckoning.” But both Jeremy and I agreed that Mark is not a villain; he’s an antihero, which is to say, his goal is good, right? He just wants to connect people. That’s good, but his methods have become perverted along the way.

	I know that when I’m writing an antihero, you can’t judge the character. You have to write the character as if they’re making their case to God why they should be allowed into heaven. Jeremy felt the same way about playing the character. He was Mark Zuckerberg’s biggest defender from the beginning — before he started shooting, during his shooting, and afterward. I didn’t read it, but I know that he wrote a letter to Mark, letting him know that he planned on playing the part respectfully and in Mark’s defense.
	
		Mikey, you have one memorable scene where Strong’s version of Mark Zuckerberg runs roughshod over your colleagues while you watch. What was it like to shoot?	

	Madison: I was excited for that scene and happy that I was able to work with Jeremy, even if just for a little bit — with me off in the corner. I had heard so much about his process, and as an actress, I’m very curious if there are things that I can learn from other actors’ processes.

	I obviously think the result of his work is very compelling, and so I was excited. I do feel like the energy that he brought to his character and like the way in which he wanted to film the scenes brought a really specific, intense energy to the environment on the set, which I think was incredibly helpful and added another layer and depth to it. And I really got to just be an observer — that’s what I was doing — and it was fascinating.

	I also noticed that — not just when the camera was on him and capturing his performance, but when it was on other people — he was still in his character, really trying to get the best performances out of everyone. That’s very generous of an actor to do that, and I really appreciated that. It was inspiring to see another actor with a process as intense and specific as that be as generous. Do you know what I mean?
	
	
		I do. There are plenty of actors who’ve been working hard and don’t give everything when the camera switches over to their costar’s shots.	

	Madison: But it’s always disappointing, too, because I really feel like you’re only as good as your counterpart. I always want the best performance out of the people I’m working with, so I was appreciative to see that.

	Sorkin: You’re the exact same way. Mikey, doing her off-camera work — you would not know that she was off-camera.
	
		Without spoiling the plot, there’s a dispiriting note at the end of the film as text on-screen informs us that some very high percentage of Americans get their news from Facebook to this day. Aaron, I think of you as an optimist — do you think there’s a way forward here?	

	Sorkin: As troubling as the climax of the film is, ultimately, you feel good at the end. It’s a feeling of optimism, because David has picked up a rock and thrown it at Goliath — and, as a matter of fact, two Davids. Frances has picked up a rock, thrown it at Facebook, and print journalism [does] too.
	
		Mikey, do you share Aaron’s optimism about pulling out from the misinformation spiral?	

	Madison: Yes, of course I do. I am ultimately a very optimistic person. I do believe in the good of people. I believe in rehabilitation and people’s ability to learn and be better. Maybe it’s a bit naive at times, but yeah, I do. We have to hold on to that hope, or else things just seem so bleak.
	
		You’re not on social media. Was there ever even the most fleeting sense, preparing for this film, that you were missing out?	

	Madison: It wasn’t a part of my preparation to be on Instagram or Facebook. It just wasn’t a part of things, and so I never indulged in that. Hearing Aaron talk about all of the dachshund videos that he was fed during his research process, there was a part of me that was like, I think I’m missing out on something there. But I’ve maintained the same feeling that me not being on social media is right, and I didn’t feel it was necessary for me to bring this character to life.
	
		Aaron, Paramount produced your film “The Trial of the Chicago 7,” before selling it to Netflix during the height of COVID. Now, they’re under new leadership, and subsuming Warner Bros. [This interview was conducted after the deal was announced, but before it closed on Oct. 6.] Do you think it’ll be more challenging, in an age of consolidation, to make films that address political issues directly?	

	Sorkin: It will be more challenging with the consolidation of Warner Bros. and Paramount. There is one less movie studio making movies, and that’s not good. Making a movie shouldn’t be considered an act of courage. It shouldn’t take bravery. But you look around, and you see studios and networks making decisions out of fear.
	

	The big reason that Frances, at the end of the movie, implores Congress to take action and pass some laws — and the reason why that’s extremely difficult to do — is that there are tech billionaires funding the campaigns of the people who need to make the laws. For that reason, it’s going to be difficult. It’s not going to be impossible.
	
		Mikey, you’ve said that you wanted to retreat from the spotlight somewhat after the burst of excitement and activity around “Anora.” What does it feel like to be back with your first film since winning the Oscar?	

	Madison: I’m very happy to be promoting this film because I really want people to go and see it, and I really believe in the story and the message. So I’m hopeful that people do go and see the movie in theaters. This was the first project I felt compelled to do after “Anora” — it felt like something very different than anything I had done before, in terms of the tone of the character and wanting to work with Aaron. It just was something that felt right.

	But in terms of the big picture, I don’t know if it’s helpful for me to think about things like that. I think I’ll get too in my head and overwhelmed. I just want to keep making movies with people I admire and doing work that feels important or compelling or moving in some way. I’m just focused on that part of it.
	
		Aaron, what made Mikey the right fit for this role? It’s so obviously different from Ani in “Anora” — and others Mikey has played, too.	

	Sorkin: Number one. You’re not going to like this, OK?

	Madison: [laughs] OK.

	Sorkin: She’s a great actor. She has world-class skills as an actor. There are certain things that an actor can’t fake. An actor can’t act smart, and an actor can’t act funny. They have to bring those things with them. Mikey has both those clubs in her golf bag. But add to that the fact that Mikey moves through the world as if everyone is right-handed and she’s left-handed. It’s just a slight … I wish I could describe it, but it’s perfect for Frances. It’s very charming. It’s very endearing. And we understand that Frances is most comfortable at her keyboard, at her computer screen. Once she has to interact face-to-face with people, it’s something she needs to make an effort to do.
	
		Given the subject matter, are you concerned that people will have preconceptions about the movie? The very point is that we live in such divided times, but, for that reason, I wonder if a movie like this can entertain the masses broadly.	

	Sorkin: People, with movies, they tend to — there are people who make up their minds without seeing it. But if you come, I bet you’ll be surprised.
	

	This interview has been condensed and edited.

schema.headline: Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on ‘The Social Reckoning’: Getting Inside a Whistleblower’s Mind, Jeremy Strong’s ‘Antihero’ Zuckerberg and Why Trump is the Movie’s Voldemort

title: ‘A Different World’ Stars Darryl M. Bell and Kadeem Hardison Launch Weekly Rewatch Podcast
description: Just in time for the revival of “A Different World” now airing on Netflix, original stars Darryl M. Bell and Kadeem Hardison — who also have major r
body:
Just in time for the revival of “A Different World” now airing on Netflix, original stars Darryl M. Bell and Kadeem Hardison — who also have major roles in the new series — are set to launch a weekly rewatch podcast. From iHeartMedia and Charlamagne Tha God’s Black Effect Podcast Network, “A Different World View with Darryl & Kadeem” will premiere next Thursday, Oct. 15. New episodes will drop every Thursday.

	“A Different World” executive producer and director Debbie Allen, who is also a part of the revival, will serve as the podcast’s first guest. Bell and Hardison will kick off their rewatch with the original series’ Season 2, Episode 2, which was Allen’s first episode with the series.
	

	Allen is known for helping transform “A Different World” under her oversight, and in the revival she is an executive producer, directed its premiere and appears as Dr. Langhorne.


	Here’s a logline for the podcast: “Each week, the pair will bring their nearly 40-year friendship and signature chemistry to conversations spanning entertainment, pop culture, sports and whatever else has their attention before heading back to Hillman. They’ll rewatch ‘A Different World’ episode by episode, sharing behind-the-scenes stories, unpacking why the groundbreaking series continues to resonate nearly four decades later and welcoming familiar faces from the show along the way. They’ll also look ahead to the new Netflix sequel series, with conversations featuring members of both the original and new casts.”



	

					Darryl M. Bell as Ron, Kadeem Hardison as Dwayne in the Netflix “A Different World” revival.
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	Hardison played Dwayne Wayne on “A Different World” while Bell was Ron Johnson Jr. The duo also appeared together in Spike Lee’s “School Daze.” More recently, they’ve toured historically Black colleges and universities as part of an “A Different World” reunion tour.
	

	“I am beyond excited to finally launch the ‘A Different World View with Darryl and Kadeem’ podcast,” said Bell in a statement. “Kadeem and I have only wanted to do this for over 25 years, and the time is now! I also could not be happier or think of better partners than Charlamagne Tha God, his team at The Black Effect and iHeartMedia.”

	Added Hardison: “I’ve been talking to this guy for 40 years. I’m so glad you all get to see what I’ve been dealing with. ‘A Different World View’ coming shortly!”

	“A Different World View with Darryl & Kadeem” is distributed by iHeartPodcasts and is part of the Black Effect Podcast Network. 

	“‘A Different World’ had an undeniable impact on Black culture, and Kadeem and Darryl are such an important part of that legacy,” said Dollie S. Bishop, president of the Black Effect Podcast Network, in a statement. “We’re excited to give them a platform to bring their friendship and comedy to listeners everywhere, sharing stories fans have never heard and celebrating the series with the generations who grew up with it and those who might just be discovering it today.”

	Here’s a trailer to “A Different World View with Darryl & Kadeem”:

schema.headline: ‘A Different World’ Stars Darryl M. Bell and Kadeem Hardison Launch Weekly Rewatch Podcast

title: Turnstile to Play Free Show at Washington Monument in Support of Humanitarian Efforts in Palestine, Sudan and Lebanon
description: Baltimore rockers Turnstile will play a free show at the Washington Monument on Saturday October 24, hosted with Human Concern International, the ba
body:
Baltimore rockers Turnstile will play a free show at the Washington Monument on Saturday October 24, hosted with Human Concern International, the band announced Thursday. The concert will raise funds to benefit their humanitarian efforts in Palestine, Sudan and Lebanon — attendees can RSVP and receive information on the show HERE and make a donation HERE.

	Hassan Wadi, Global Director of Human Concern International, said, “As a Gazan, I cannot be prouder of the Turnstile team and community for coming together to support the people of Gaza, Lebanon and Sudan. Three regions who have suffered so much. With your support we aim to provide food, water, medical care and shelter to families in need in all three regions. Thank you all for your support, we are honored to collect and deliver these donations.”
	

	The concert will be the final date of the band’s “Never Enough Tour Part 2,” which launched with a free show in Baltimore in May of 2025, although there will be a festival performance at Tyler, the Creator’s Camp Flog Gnaw event in Los Angeles next month.  

	The band recently were musical guests on “Saturday Night Live,” performing fiery versions of “Birds” and “I Care/Dull.” They released “Never Enough: Versions,” a reimagining of songs from their Grammy-winning “Never Enough” album with contributions from Elton John, Slayyyter, Dying Fetus, Porches, Hayley Williams, A. G. Cook, Floating Points, Rod Lee, Kettama, Mustafa, Julien Baker, Panda Bear, Brandon Woody, Four Tet, Dan Deacon, Blood Orange, Chanel Beads, Faye Webster, Angel Du$t, Shabaka, Oklou, Nourished By Time, and Alex G.
	

	NEVER ENOUGH TOUR PT. 2

title: CBS Vampire Sitcom ‘Eternally Yours’ Is a Genial Riff on ‘Ghosts’: TV Review
description: The CBS sitcom “Eternally Yours” is not officially a spinoff of the network’s hit series “Ghosts.” But, functionally, that’s the pitch. Another stor
body:
The CBS sitcom “Eternally Yours” is not officially a spinoff of the network’s hit series “Ghosts.” But, functionally, that’s the pitch. Another story of supernatural roommates from the same creative team, “Eternally Yours” swaps out specters for vampires. With only a single, 22-minute episode sent to critics, it’s too early to tell whether “Eternally Yours” will differentiate itself from the de facto parent show. It also may not be trying to — and fans of “Ghosts,” of which there are many, may not mind.
	

	Joe Port and Joe Weisman, who developed “Ghosts” from the British original and now showrun the American remake, technically conceived of (and pitched!) “Eternally Yours” first. Still, the version that’s made it to air has so many obvious echoes that this bit of trivia remains just that: trivial. Unlike ghosts, vampires have physical form and can interact directly with humans; like ghosts, vampires live forever, allowing for a humorous juxtaposition of characters from many points in time in one unhappy household.


	Here, our cast of characters is led by Charles (Ed Weeks) and Liz (Allegra Edwards), a couple who’ve been together since he sank his fangs into her 500 years ago but whose marriage has now curdled into endless bickering. (The throat clearing she once thought a cutesy quirk is now an unbearable nuisance.) Joining them in their Seattle coven — they admit “Twilight” was onto something with the year-round cloud cover in the Pacific Northwest, if not the “stay together forever” thing — is Jesse (Parker Young), a personal trainer straight out of the ‘80s who uses a spray tan to show up in mirrors. Jesse’s human wife, Phyllis (Rose Abdoo of “Hacks”), has a brain made of Swiss cheese from the constant mind wipes. That hasn’t stopped them from having two teenage, half-vampire sons, which begs some questions about vampire physiology but allows for some solid jokes about superpowered adolescence.
	

	Clearly, “Ghosts” isn’t the only influence at work here: Any vampire comedy, especially one about co-habitation, (night)walks in the footsteps of “What We Do in the Shadows,” the mockumentary turned six-season FX show. But where “Shadows” was absurdist and made frequent use of handheld cameras, “Eternally Yours” is a broadcast comedy in its bones. In lieu of testimonials, there’s a “How I Met Your Mother”-esque voiceover from Max (Jaren Lewison), a human who’s horrified to discover his girlfriend Emma (Helen J. Shen) has good reason not to introduce him to her parents. Emma is Charles and Liz’s adopted daughter, because while vampires can procreate with humans, they can’t with each other. Don’t look for consistent logic from a show that lets Weeks and Edwards keep their respective British and American accents despite playing Romanians!

	“Eternally Yours” gets a few good gags into the pilot: Charles and Liz once got couples’ therapy from Sigmund Freud himself in a cutaway flashback, and Charles’ nihilism in the face of eternal, often miserable life is an amusing trait. (He slips and tells one human that “you get to die.”) But the show needs more time to carve out its own identity, both vis-a-vis “Ghosts” and in the crowded field of vampire media. Luckily, if there’s one thing vampires have in spades, it’s time to kill — get it?

	“Eternally Yours” will premiere on Oct. 8 at 8:30 p.m. ET on CBS and Paramount+.

title: Variety to Honor John Turturro With the Creative Vanguard Award at Miami Film Festival
description: Emmy Award-winning actor, writer and director John Turturro will be honored with the Variety Creative Vanguard Award at Miami Dade College’s (MDC) M
body:
Emmy Award-winning actor, writer and director John Turturro will be honored with the Variety Creative Vanguard Award at Miami Dade College’s (MDC) Miami Film Festival GEMS on Monday, Nov. 2. 

	The event will take place at Miami Dade College Wolfson Auditorium at 7:00 p.m. The honor will be for Turturro’s achievements over more than four decades in the industry across film, theater and television. His upcoming film “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan, will screen at the festival on Oct. 29, ahead of its wide release in theaters beginning on Oct. 30. The 13th Miami Film Festival Gems is scheduled Oct. 29 through Nov. 5 and will continue its tradition of celebrating this year’s top films and award contenders.
	

	Turturro will participate in a Q&A about his work with Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh. “It’s fitting that John Turturro made his acting debut in an uncredited role in ‘Raging Bull’ without saying a word of dialogue,” said Setoodeh. “For nearly 50 years, his mere presence has been proof that audiences are in for something special. With a body of work that spans film, TV and theater – from ‘Barton Fink’ to ‘The Big Lebowski,’ ‘Severance’ to ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ – there’s nothing he can’t do. His fearless approach to the craft makes him the perfect recipient of the Variety Creative Vanguard Award.”


	“We are thrilled to welcome John Turturro to GEMS and celebrate his remarkable body of work with Variety‘s Creative Vanguard Award. From his unforgettable performances throughout his career to his latest turn in ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ John continues to bring an unmatched depth and authenticity to every role he takes on. His work has inspired generations of filmmakers, and we’re honored to recognize his enduring impact on American cinema at this year’s festival,” said Lauren Cohen, Director of Programming at Miami Film Festival.
	

	John Turturro’s career spans more than four decades. His acclaimed film credits include “Do the Right Thing,” “The Big Lebowski,” “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” “Miller’s Crossing,” “Barton Fink,” “The Batman” and “Quiz Show,” for which he received a Golden Globe nomination. On television, Turturro won an Emmy Award for his guest appearance on Monk and received Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations for “The Night Of” and “Severance.” Turturro received the Caméra d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival for “Mac,” his directorial debut. His other films as writer and director include “Illuminata,” “Romance & Cigarettes,” “Passione” and “Fading Gigolo.” Turturro starred as Mickey Sabbath in his and Ariel Levy’s stage adaptation of Philip Roth’s novel “Sabbath’s Theater” in 2023 and recently starred as Berenger in the adaptation by A.R.T of Eugène Ionesco’s play “Rhinoceros” with Paul Giamatti & Tatiana Maslany, directed by Diane Paulus.

	Miami Dade College celebrates cinema in two annual events, Miami Dade College’s Miami Film Festival GEMS (Oct. 29-Nov. 5) and Miami Film Festival (44th annual edition, April 1-11, 2027). The Miami Film Festival is considered the preeminent film festival for showcasing Ibero-American cinema in the U.S. and a major launch pad for all international and documentary cinema. The annual Festival welcomes more than 45,000 audience members and more than 400 filmmakers, producers, talent and industry professionals. In the last five years, the Festival has screened films from more than 60 countries, including 300 World, International, North American, U.S. and East Coast Premieres. The Festival also offers unparalleled educational opportunities to film students and the community at large. 

	For more information, visit http://www.miamifilmfestival.com/

title: Why Gary Vaynerchuk Is Putting Everything Into Collectibles Brand ‘VeeFriends’: ‘It Could Be the Biggest Business I Ever Build in My Life’
description: From Resy to Empathy Wines, VaynerX chairman Gary “GaryVee” Vaynerchuk knows how to build a profitable business. But up until now, the serial entrep
body:
From Resy to Empathy Wines, VaynerX chairman Gary “GaryVee” Vaynerchuk knows how to build a profitable business. But up until now, the serial entrepreneur and YouTube star’s work has been based largely on impersonal ideas. 

	Enter VeeFriends, the business that Vaynerchuk has wanted to own since he was a kid.

	On its face, VeeFriends is a brand that aims to “fill a gap in the collectibles” market. Run by Vaynerchuk as founder and CEO, VeeFriends is a storytelling universe that includes more than 280 hand-drawn characters, each designed to teach kindness and life lessons across both younger and older generations.
	

	Influenced by the work of Jim Henson and Walt Disney described as a cross between Pokémon and “Sesame Street,” Vaynerchuk’s the VeeFriends brand launched in 2021 and now spans comic books, collectibles, content, trading cards and purposeful storytelling.




	

	



	“From a business standpoint, I think it’s the biggest business I’m building. I believe intellectual property is the winner of the next half century,” Vaynerchuk, who boasts nearly 5 million subscribers to his YouTube channel, tells Variety. “It’s an eight-figure business already in revenue, selling trading cards, coins this year. That’s a meaningful business. I think it could be the biggest business I ever build in my life. Genuinely in my heart, I view it as Disney, Marvel, Pokemon. I’d be surprised if this isn’t where I end up at some point in my career. Meaning, with all my 13 different businesses, if you ask me, you got to pick one — restaurant group, all these alternative sports, the advertising agency is huge, the wine business — if I had to pick a horse where I think I’m riding on just one in my 60s, 70s, 80s, I think it’s VeeFriends.”
	

	At New York Comic Con this week, Vaynerchuk is unveiling the brand’s biggest product expansion yet through digital and physical collectible content, including the reveal of “VeeFriends” issue #22, “Gentle Giant.”

	Featuring cover art by Rob Liefeld, “Gentle Giant” is set against the paranoia of the Cold War and tells the story of a secret government experiment to create the ultimate supersoldier using ancient giant DNA. But when the 20-foot-tall creation awakens, his gentle nature clashes with the violent purpose he was built for. Part sci-fi thriller, part Frankenstein story, the issue explores what happens when a living weapon begins to seem more human than the people controlling him.

	“Gentle Giant is fighting against this count, Mindful Minakawa, that we set up a couple of episodes of comic books ago and it’s the story of in the 1940s about the U.S. and Japan this is made for 35 to 65 year old history nerds that like characters,” Vaynerchuk says. “That’s fitting good old classic comic book nostalgia: King Kong versus Godzilla, Superman, Cold War-era storytelling. But then Considerate Cowboy is going to come out in the future, and that’s going to be a romance novel. That’s going to be for women. One of the cool things I did, and it was very selfish, but it was also on strategy, is by creating 280-plus characters, I will never run out of time telling my stories.” 



	

	





	

	



	As he builds up a transmedia and merch business, Vaynerchuk says isn’t looking for every VeeFriend to be appealing to every demographic — he’s looking to create one VeeFriend that each person can connect with.

	“VeeFriends, as a whole, is looking to be [a brand for ages] six to 106. But each individual character and each individual execution may be looking at different demos,” Vaynerchuk says. “I’ll give you an example: when Batman puts out a Lego Batman movie, and it’s clearly made for seven or eight year olds, that’s very different from ‘Dark Knight,’ a feature film that’s rated R. That’s how I think at VeeFriends. I want it to truly be six to 106. All genders, races, income levels, regions in the world. Not everything’s going to be based on just English or Americana. So, it’s an incredibly vast playground of creativity that I’m enjoying.”
	

	Vaynerchuk describes VeeFriends as his greatest passion project — but also the one he thinks will be the most profitable of his ventures in the end, for both “selfish and selfless” reasons, similar to how he approached building his own personal “GaryVee” brand on social media.

	“It has the highest financial upside, but it’s selfless because I’m also incredibly driven by making it known because I think I can do good in the world if it’s known and I think it’s very similar to what I ended up doing with GaryVee,” Vaynerchuk says. “I built my personal brand as a business move 15 years ago before people saw it, and it was the most selfish and selfless thing. It’s led to a lot of economic opportunity, but it’s also led to me impacting millions of people in a very positive way. I think there’s just a lot of people out there spewing a lot of hate and negativity and I know that people consume my content for a reprieve from all this darkness.”

	There are plans for much more VeeFriends content, though Vaynerchuk is mindful of growing in a way that makes consumers comfortable — and that includes limiting the use of generative AI, for the time being. 

	“We ourselves have not really fully executed,” Vaynerchuk says, noting that all the VeeFriends characters to date have been created by himself and the VeeFriends team. “A lot of the consumer doesn’t want you to. We more use it for project management and efficiencies more so than the output. But I do predict very easily that the stigma will go away within the next decade, and we’ll be prepared to make content at scale with it once we think the world would appreciate it.”

title: A+E Global Media and Lifetime Expand Microdrama Slate, Announcing Mobile Launch Originals and Nearly 200 Titles Adapted for Third-Party Distribution
description:
A+E Global Media and Lifetime are dramatically expanding their output in the world of microdramas and vertical video. 

	The company has announced t
body:
A+E Global Media and Lifetime are dramatically expanding their output in the world of microdramas and vertical video. 

	The company has announced that its new MyLifetime.com platform will offer three original Lifetime vertical films from Microhouse Films as well as seven titles adapted from the A+E Global Media library.

	The Lifetime mobile app plans to add new vertical titles every two weeks (along with access on MyLifetime.com), with up to seven originals by the end of the year. Two of those will be sponsored holiday-themed verticals from vertTV.
	

	“Microdramas are one of the most dynamic and exciting areas of growth in entertainment, and Lifetime is proud to be an early and meaningful participant in that evolution,” said Elaine Frontain Bryant, executive vice president and head of programming, A&E, Lifetime and LMN, in a statement. “Our opportunity is not simply to introduce a new format, but to define its role within the Lifetime ecosystem in a way that strengthens our brand, deepens fandom and gives audiences another way to experience the stories they already love. With original series, library titles and new brand-supported projects rolling out through the Lifetime app on mobile and MyLifetime.com, we are building a strategy that spans premium storytelling, audience engagement and global distribution.”


	Also, timed to the upcoming MIPCOM market, A+E Global Media has adapted nearly 200 titles into vertical microdramas that will be available to license to other platforms.

	The Microhouse Films slate for MyLifetime.com includes “Tides of Temptation,” “Matched With a Murderer” and “His Lies Taste Like Love.”
	

	“Tides of Temptation,” which is exec produced by Taye Diggs, Autumn Federici and Shelby Stone, is a stand-alone digital companion to the Lifetime original movie “Terry McMillan Presents: Paradise with You,” which debuts Nov. 7.

	Other Microhouse Films projects to come include “Reunion Island,” which debuts at the New York-based microdrama/vertical storytelling-based ALZA Festival, and “Recklessly in Love with My Daughter’s Best Man.”

	The holiday-themed, sponsored vertical originals from vertTV include “Casting Christmas” and “Destination, Christmas.” Jeffrey Schenck, Barry Barnholtz, Peter Sullivan, Brian Nolan and Ben Rosenthal are the founders of vertTV.

	Meanwhile, Lifetime original films that have been edited into vertical chapters for MyLifetime.com include “A Lifeguard’s Obsession,” “Burned by Love,” “Danger in the House,” “My Husband’s Worse Mistake,” “What Would You Kill For?,” “Secret of a Dean’s Wife” and “College Professor Obsession.”

	As for the A+E library content that has also been cut into microseries, besides the nearly 200 Lifetime movies, it includes “Cold Case Files,” “I Survived,” “Alone,” “Ice Road Truckers,” “Forged in Fire,” “History’s Greatest Mysteries,” “Hoarders” and “Married at First Sight.”

	“The expansion into vertical storytelling creates compelling new opportunities for brands to connect with audiences in highly engaging, mobile-first environments,” said Toby Byrne, A+E Global Media’s president of media solutions, in a statement. “Projects like these give advertisers the ability to participate in premium, culturally relevant storytelling while reaching audiences across the platforms where they are spending their time.”

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle Reportedly Begged Trump Donor To Send $100K To Her Amex Account
description:
Kimberly Guilfoyle to Trump Donor
                          'Honey Please' Wire $100K To My Amex
body:
Kimberly Guilfoyle to Trump Donor
                          'Honey Please' Wire $100K To My Amex Account
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kimberly Guilfoyle reportedly begged a Trump donor to wire $100K straight to her American Express account ... messaging him "Honey please" as part of her plea.
      
    
            According to Signal messages reviewed by the Wall Street Journal, Donald Trump Jr.'s ex-fiancée was messaging former Kentucky congressional candidate Eric Deters in July 2025 when she made an urgent request for a payment that wouldn't leave a paper trail.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Guilfoyle was allegedly trying to get Deters to pay down her credit card balance before her congressional hearing to become the U.S. ambassador to Greece.
      

            On July 3, just 6 days before her July 9 hearing, she reportedly messaged him ... "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
      
    
            She then sent Deters a PDF with instructions for paying an AmEx bill, telling him ... "You could just send it here."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Guilfoyle added ... "It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express."
      
    
            Deters didn't end up paying, telling her it would ruin his marriage.
      
    
            Guilfoyle and Deters were messaging for months before the financial request, the WSJ reports ... Deters was seeking Guilfoyle's help in getting the Trump administration to take a look at his personal tax and legal issues. He reportedly promised Guilfoyle up to $1 million if she succeeded.
      
    
            He says Guilfoyle told him, "I will be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever" if he ponied up the dough to pay her American Express bill ... but he told the WSJ she never got him out of his jam.
      
    
            We reached out to Guilfoyle's camp ... so far, no word back.

title: 5-Year-Old Boy Dead After Large Video Display Board Falls on Him at Florida School
description:
5-Year-Old Boy
                          Dies After Display Board Lands On Him at School
body:
5-Year-Old Boy
                          Dies After Display Board Lands On Him at School
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 8, 2026
                            5:34 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 8, 2026
                                6:44 AM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A 5-year-old boy lost his life Wednesday after a large video display board reportedly came crashing down on him at a Florida school.
      
    
            Cops say the tragic incident occurred around noon at Riviera Elementary School in Palm Bay, FL, which is nearly 175 miles north of Miami.
      
    
            Palm Bay PD Deputy Chief Nick Szczepanski told reporters that school staff quickly called 911 and administered first aid to the severely injured boy as police and paramedics raced to the scene.
      
    
            The boy, identified by his family as Bellamy Dawkins-Morris, was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
      

            Szczepanski said, "On the surface, this appears to be a tragic accident," but detectives from the Special Victims Unit were still "actively investigating" the case.
      
    
            The Palm Bay police and Brevard Public Schools -- which oversees Riviera Elementary -- have not indicated how the display board fell on Bellamy. However, Bellamy's family told a local news outlet that the boy was moving the display board when it tipped over and fell on him.
      
    
            Bellamy's great-aunt, Miriam Rodriguez, also said she expected the child to be safe and secure at the school, but "he didn't return to us.” Rodriguez added, “My emotions, my sadness has subsided, and I am angry. We need answers, and we need them immediately.”
      
    
            Dr. Mark Rendell, the district's superintendent, called it an "incredibly difficult day" while reminding everyone that "we lost a life today, a precious young life, and there are no words to describe that loss."
      
    
            Rendell said he met with Bellamy's family and "couldn't find the words to share with them my grief and the grief that all of us have."

                            5:12 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Halle Berry has completed a mandatory parenting program as she battles ex-husband Olivier Martinez over custody of their son ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Berry signed a certificate Tuesday verifying she completed the Los Angeles Superior Court's "Our Children First" online mediation orientation and parent education program.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Per the court's website, parents are required to complete the court's online child custody mediation orientation and parent education program, officially known as "Our Children First," before moving forward with custody or visitation disputes.
      

            The filing comes amid the former couple's explosive legal battle over their 13-year-old son, Maceo.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Olivier accused Halle of putting Maceo in a headlock and choking him while he was playing a virtual reality game. Halle denied the allegation, saying they were playfully roughhousing and insisting she never put her hands around his neck.
      
    
            Halle has called herself a domestic violence victim and advocate not a perpetrator and said she would never hurt their child. She also accused Olivier of failing to provide Maceo with appropriate boundaries and resisting professional help for the boy's behavioral and neurodivergent issues.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A judge previously granted Olivier's request for a temporary restraining order, while allowing Halle to maintain final decision making authority over Maceo's mental health and education.
      
    
            The former couple is scheduled to return to court October 16.

description:
Manson Family Killer
                          Recommended For Parole ...
body:
Manson Family Killer
                          Recommended For Parole ...
                          Ball's In Newsom's Court
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 8, 2026
                            7:35 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Charles Manson family killer Patricia Krenwinkel is on the doorstep of freedom after being recommended for parole in California ... but Governor Gavin Newsom could still step in and keep her locked up.
      
    
            Krenwinkel, who was among the Manson family members convicted in the Tate-LaBianca murders in 1969, was granted parole on a preliminary basis Tuesday ... according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.
      
    
            It's the third time 78-year-old Krenwinkel has been approved for parole ... Newsom used his power to prevent her release the previous two times ... and it will be interesting to see if he does so again or if the third time's the charm for Krenwinkel.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Krenwinkel's parole decision will become final only after review by the Board of Parole Hearings and Newsom.
      
    
            Prosecutors in Los Angeles County reportedly plan to encourage Newsom to keep Krenwinkel in prison.
      
    
            She's locked up at the California Institution for Women in Corona ... and she's been behind bars for going on 56 years now, making her the longest-serving female in the California prison system.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Krenwinkel was convicted in 1971 for the murders of Sharon Tate, Jay Sebring, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski, and Steven Parent ... plus Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary.
      
    
            Newsom's got presidential aspirations ... so this is a big decision.
      
    
            Stay tuned ...
